chunks: "I attack it from both sides: make the ground impedance low, and make the currents flowing through it small and local.
For impedance, I use a solid, unbroken ground plane on the layer right next to the signal layers, with a thin dielectric so the loop inductance is tiny.
I avoid slots, splits and neck-downs, I don't let via fields or connector keep-outs cut the plane, and I stitch layers with ground vias wherever signals change layers and around the edges.
Connectors get lots of ground pins interleaved with signals, because each pin is about ten nanohenries.
For the currents, I put decoupling capacitors right at the pins so the fast current loops close locally and don't spread through the plane.
I keep switching regulators' hot loops tiny. I limit simultaneous switching with slower edges, series resistors or staggered timing, and use enough supply and ground pins.
Then I partition by placement: power stage and digital on one side, sensitive analog on the other, with the ADC at the boundary, so noisy return currents never cross quiet circuits.
And I put ground probe points on the board to verify it.
I usually budget it numerically: if I want under half an LSB of error, I work back to how many milliohms and nanohenries I can afford."
